1	# Per-paper extraction instructions, v6 (GP-RareLink; Claude Code route, D-20)
2	
3	*Changes from v2 come from the Stage 3 findings (`reports/poc_stage3_findings.md`) and decision D-22, marked "(v3)". Changes from v3 come from the Stage 3b findings (`reports/poc_stage3b_findings.md`) and decisions D-23 and D-24, marked "(v4)". The changes from v4 are D-27 and D-29 (Jimmy, 2026-10-19), from the Stage 5 audit (`reports/poc_stage4_5_findings.md` §10), marked "(v5)". v5 was checked on 20 HA20 papers under D-29 (`poc-ha20-v5-subset`). The change from v5 is D-31 (Jimmy, 2026-10-19), from the re-audit (`reports/poc_stage4_5_findings.md` §10.7), marked "(v6)": no positional reading of stacked cells. v6 is the candidate for the frozen pipeline; it has not been run.*
4	
5	You extract structured evidence from **one** published paper for a literature-curation study of A20 haploinsufficiency (HA20), the disease caused by germline *TNFAIP3* variants. Your output is checked by script (every quote must be found verbatim in the paper) and then by a separate reviewer, so accuracy and honest abstention matter more than completeness.
6	
7	## Inputs (paths are given in your task)
8	
9	1. **The paper**: a Markdown file converted from the PMC or Europe PMC full text. Its first lines give the PMID and title. Merged table cells are repeated in every row and column they cover.
10	   - **(v3)** The file may end with a `## Supplementary material` section converted from the files published with the article. Treat it as part of the paper and quote it verbatim like any other text.
11	   - Some supplementary files are excerpts, with `[...]` marking omitted lines. Never join text across `[...]`.
12	   - **(v4)** In tables converted from supplementary files, ` / ` separates values that were stacked on separate lines inside one cell (see "Stacked cells" below; changed in v6).
13	2. **The schema**: `pipeline/extract/claude_code/schema_ha20_v5.json`. It defines five tables, their fields, types, allowed values, and a description for each.
14	3. **The rules**: `pipeline/extract/sliders_adapter/prompts/extraction_rules_v1.md`. Apply all nine. Where this file is more specific (scope, labels, table symbols), this file wins.
15	
16	**What you may read.** Read only these three files.
17	- Do not open any other file in the repository.
18	- Do not use web search or web fetch.
19	- Do not use anything you remember about this paper, its authors, its patients, the gene or the variants.
20	
21	**What counts as missing.** If the paper doesn't say it, the value is missing (see "Values" below).
22	
23	## Scope: who gets a row (v3, D-22)
24	
25	- **In scope:**
26	  - every person the paper describes who has a *TNFAIP3* variant or an HA20 (A20 haploinsufficiency) diagnosis;
27	  - relatives the paper describes in relation to such a person, whether tested (including tested negative) or affected.
28	- **Out of scope:** other members of a cohort, for example patients whose variants are in other genes, or who have no variant. They get **no** rows. Record the study's total number of patients, as the authors state it, in `publications.cohort_size_as_stated`.
29	- **People from summaries of earlier reports are in scope** when they meet the rule above: a literature table in a case report, or a review describing individuals. Each gets its own row, with `source_reference_in_review` filled verbatim.
30	  - **(v4)** A previously published person mentioned only in passing (for example one sentence in the Discussion) is in scope only when the paper gives at least one individual-level fact about that person beyond the diagnosis: sex, age, variant or a feature.
31	  - **(v4, D-23)** When a table has a per-patient reference or source column, copy that cell into `source_reference_in_review` for each patient, also in cohort and survey papers. Do not leave it only in `method_note`; the cross-paper merge depends on it.
32	- **Variants in other genes:**
33	  - record one only for an in-scope person, and only when the paper attributes it to that person unambiguously;
34	  - do not list risk alleles or polygenic-score variants;
35	  - **(v4)** do not create a row for a variant the paper names but does not describe (no printed variant), for example "variants in PIK3R1 and HBB";
36	  - if the attribution is contradictory, leave it out and say so in `method_note`.
37	- **(v4) Other variant rows to leave out:** common variants the authors dismiss as non-causal (for example a frequent SNP they call benign), and variants found only in tumour tissue (somatic).
38	- **(v4) Mosaic carriers:** a person with a germline mosaic *TNFAIP3* variant is in scope; record zygosity `mosaic`.
39	- **`reports_individuals_with_tnfaip3_variant`** is `true` only when the paper describes at least one identifiable in-scope person, that is, with any individual-level detail. A paper that mentions such patients only as counts or at group level gets `false`.
40	
41	## Labels (v3, D-22)
42	
43	Choose each person's `individual_label_in_paper` by the first rule that applies, so that two independent extractions give the same label:
44	1. **The paper's own label**, verbatim, in the form it uses most often (e.g. `P1`, `Patient 3`, `II-2`).
45	2. **A relative without an own label:** `<relation as written> of <label of the related person>` (e.g. `mother of P1`, `sister of patient`).
46	3. **A table row without a label column:** `Table <n> row <k>`, with k counting data rows from the top (e.g. `Table 2 row 3`).
47	4. **A previously published person described in the text without a label:** `ref <reference as printed> patient` (e.g. `ref [12] patient`). Add ` 2`, ` 3` for further people from the same reference, in order of mention.
48	5. **The single unnamed patient of a case report:** `patient`.
49	6. **Otherwise:** `unnamed person <k>`, in order of first mention.
50	
51	**(v4) Additions:**
52	- **Patients as table columns:** `Table <n> column <k>`, with k counting data columns from the left.
53	- **A table column of bare numbers that index the patients** (values like 1, 2, 3 under a heading such as "No.", "Case" or "Patient number"): `Table <n> #<value>` (e.g. `Table 3 #1`). If the values are labels such as "P1" or "Case 2", or the text uses its own label for that person, rule 1 applies.
54	- **The same label in two families** (e.g. two people called "IV:1"): `<label> (Family <n>)`.
55	- **Role words are not labels.** "The proband", "the index case" or "our patient" do not count as the paper's own label; use rule 5 or 6.
56	- **Relatives without a stated sex:** when the paper says only "parents", "children" or "siblings", write `parent of X`, `child of X` or `sibling of X` (and `parent of X 2` for the second). Never guess "mother" or "brother".
57	- A made-up label (rules 3–6) still needs a span: quote the text where the person first appears.
58	
59	Use the identical label in every table for the same person.
60	
61	## Output: one JSON file, at the path given in your task
62	
63	```json
64	{
65	  "pmid": "<from the paper's header line>",
66	  "instructions_version": "extract_v6",
67	  "reports_individuals_with_tnfaip3_variant": true,
68	  "relevance_note": "<one sentence, with a short quote, saying why>",
69	  "method_note": "<how you worked, e.g. whether a script transcribed a table; list any contradictions you found in the paper>",
70	  "tables": {
71	    "publications": [ROW],
72	    "individuals": [ROW, ...],
73	    "variants": [ROW, ...],
74	    "phenotypic_features": [ROW, ...],
75	    "phenotype_checklist": [ROW, ...]
76	  }
77	}
78	```
79	
80	A **ROW** is an object with every field of that table, using the field names exactly as in the schema. Each field maps to a **cell**:
81	
82	```json
83	{"value": <value>, "span": "<exact quote from the paper>"}
84	```
85	
86	### Values
87	- **Type.** Use the schema's type for each field. Enum fields take only the listed strings.
88	- **Missing values.** Follow each field's schema description.
89	  - Where the description says "null", use `{"value": null, "span": null}`.
90	  - Otherwise, text and enum fields take `{"value": "not reported", "span": null}`, and numeric, date and boolean fields take `{"value": null, "span": null}`.
91	- **`pmid` fields.** The value comes from the header line; the span is that header line, e.g. `"PMID: 12345678"`.
92	- **`*_iso8601` fields.** These are your conversion of the matching original-text field. Give them only when the original text states a number, and use the same span as the original-text field.
93	- **`hpo_label_candidate` and `hpo_id_candidate`.** These are your suggestions. Give an ID only if you are sure of it; otherwise null. Their span is `null`.
94	- **`checklist_feature`.** The span is `null`, because the names come from the schema.
95	- **Age at diagnosis.** Record it in `age_at_diagnosis_*`. Don't put it in onset or last evaluation.
96	
97	### Spans
98	- **Every non-missing value needs a span**, except the fields listed just above.
99	- **Copy exactly.** A span is copied character for character from the paper Markdown, including unusual spaces and symbols. Never paraphrase, correct or join text that isn't contiguous.
100	- **Keep it short.** Use the smallest sentence fragment, table cell or table-row segment that supports the value. That is normally under 300 characters.
101	- **Tables with patients as rows.** Quote a contiguous piece of the row from the patient label through the cell.
102	- **Tables with patients as columns.** Quote the row from its row label through that patient's cell, e.g. `| Sex | F | M` for the second patient column. Name the column header once in `method_note`.
103	- **Multiple places.** If support sits in several places, `span` may be a list of exact quotes:
104	  - up to **five** for `treatment_summary`, `functional_evidence_statement`, `parental_testing_statement` and `clinical_diagnosis_basis`;
105	  - up to **three** for any other field.
106	
107	### Rows
108	- **`publications`:** exactly one row for this paper.
109	- **`individuals`:** one row per in-scope person (see Scope), labelled by the Labels rules.
110	- **`variants`:** one row per (person, variant).
111	  - `variant_original_string` is the **shortest** contiguous text giving the variant, not a whole sentence. Put the transcript, cDNA and protein parts in their own fields.
112	  - **(v3)** If the paper ties a *TNFAIP3* variant to the person but prints no variant description (only in a figure or an unavailable supplement), keep the row with `variant_original_string` = `"not reported"`. Never fill it from memory.
113	- **`phenotypic_features`:** one row per feature the paper explicitly reports present (`observed`) or explicitly reports absent (`excluded`) for that person. No rows for features the paper doesn't mention.
114	- **`phenotype_checklist`:** for **every** individual, one row for **each** of the 20 checklist features in the schema's description of that table, using the names exactly as listed there. Status is `observed`, `excluded` or `not reported` under rule 4.
115	
116	### Absence and evidence basis (D-21, D-22)
117	- **`evidence_basis` is required** on every `phenotypic_features` row, and on every checklist row whose status is not `not reported`.
118	- **Group statements.** You may mark a feature `excluded` for a person from a statement about a group **only when the statement names the group explicitly**, e.g. "only Pt3 of the four patients had recurrent fevers". Such rows take `evidence_basis = "inferred from group statement"`.
119	  - Counts without names ("arthritis in 2/4") do not exclude anyone.
120	- **(v3) Table symbols.** A `-`, `–`, `0`, `N` or similar cell counts as `excluded` only when the paper's legend or text defines that symbol as absent or negative.
121	  - Quote that definition as a second span next to the cell.
122	  - Otherwise the cell is `not reported` (rule 6). Empty cells, `NA` and `ND` are always `not reported`.
123	- **(v3) Study criteria are not evidence.** Never use a study's inclusion or exclusion criteria (e.g. "patients with malignancy were excluded") to mark a feature for a person.
124	- **Narrow and broad features.** A narrower absence never excludes a broader checklist item. "No arthritis" does not exclude "arthritis or arthralgia"; leave that item `not reported` unless arthralgia is also addressed. The same applies to other composite items, e.g. "skin lesions (rash, folliculitis, erythema nodosum)".
125	- **(v5, D-27) Normal findings.** When the paper reports a finding as normal or negative for a person ("CRP was normal", "normal C3 and C4 levels", "ANA negative"), record the abnormality it rules out as the feature and mark it `excluded`: `feature_text_as_stated` = "elevated CRP", "low complement", "positive ANA". Keep the paper's own words in the span ("CRP was normal"). Name only an abnormality the finding measures; a normal examination or investigation as a whole ("gastrointestinal investigation was negative") excludes nothing more specific than what it names, so write it as the paper does and say so in `method_note`.
126	- **(v4) Zero counts.** A count of 0 in a table of counts (e.g. "0" or "0/2" in a column for a disease group) excludes no one, like any count without names. Text that names the group ("none of the patients had uveitis") still excludes.
127	- **(v6, D-31) Stacked cells.** A cell with several values separated by ` / ` lists values that were stacked on separate lines (often one per patient). **Do not assign them to people by position**, even when the number of values equals the number of people. Use a stacked value for a person only when the paper labels it for that person (for example "P1: 18 / P2: 24", or a sentence naming the person and the value). Otherwise record the field or checklist item as `not reported` for each person in that row, and say in `method_note` which table and columns were stacked. A value the same for every person in the row, printed once (not stacked), is not affected.
128	- **Contradictions inside the paper.** If the paper says both that a person has a feature and that they don't:
129	  - emit both `phenotypic_features` rows, each with its own span;
130	  - set that checklist item to `not reported`;
131	  - list the contradiction in `method_note`.
132	
133	### Variant fields belong to this person's variant (v5, D-29)
134	Zygosity, inheritance, variant type, pathogenicity, ACMG criteria and functional evidence describe **one person's variant**. Fill them only from:
135	- this person's own table row or column, or a sentence that names this person or this exact variant; or
136	- a statement about a **named group that includes this person** and gives one value for all of them ("all six patients carried heterozygous variants").
137	
138	Leave the field `not reported` (with span null) when:
139	- the statement is about the cohort's or the paper's variants in general, without naming a group this person is clearly in ("the variants were classified as pathogenic");
140	- the statement lists several values for a group ("splice-site, frameshift and nonsense variants"): it does not say which one is this person's;
141	- the paper gives this person a different or open status elsewhere: a variant not identified or not determined, a mosaic or somatic finding, a VUS, a relative not tested. A group statement never overrides that;
142	- the value is about another person's variant, for example a relative carrying the proband's variant, unless the paper says it for the relative.
143	
144	Variant type: record only a class the paper states for this variant (or for a named group of variants that includes it). Do not derive it from the HGVS string.
145	
146	### Inheritance (v4, D-24)
147	- **De novo:** only when the paper states parental testing with the variant absent in both parents (rule 8).
148	- **Inherited:** record `inherited maternal` or `inherited paternal` when the paper states that the named parent carries the same variant, even if it never uses the word "inherited". Quote that statement in `parental_testing_statement`. Use `inherited unspecified parent` when it says a parent carries it without saying which.
149	- **Otherwise:** `not reported`. Do not infer from a pedigree drawing or from an affected but untested parent.
150	- This is more specific than rule 8, so it wins.
151	
152	### When the paper describes no in-scope person
153	For example, a review without patient-level detail, or a paper about something else:
154	- set `reports_individuals_with_tnfaip3_variant` to `false`;
155	- fill the `publications` row;
156	- leave the other tables empty.

158	### Large papers
159	If the output is long, you may build it in parts with a short Python script and combine the parts.
160	- Every value must still come from your reading of the paper.
161	- If a script transcribes a table, check its output against the table and say so in `method_note`.
162	- Use only your own scratch directory (given in your task) for temporary files.

1	Extraction rules (GP-RareLink, v1). These rules apply to every table and every row.
2	
3	1. Use only the supplied document. Do not use outside knowledge about the gene, the disease, specific variants or specific patients. If the document does not state something, the value is "not reported" (for text fields) or null (for numeric and date fields). Never fill a gap from memory.
4	2. Every value must be supported by a verbatim quote copied exactly from the document. Do not paraphrase inside the quote. If no exact quote supports a value, do not emit the value.
5	3. Keep original strings. Record variant descriptions, ages, feature names and labels exactly as printed. Never convert protein-only variant descriptions into cDNA notation, never add a transcript that is not printed, never translate units.
6	4. Three-state phenotypes: a feature is "observed" only when the document says the person has or had it, and "excluded" only when the document explicitly says it was absent, negative or not found in that person. Silence is "not reported". Never turn silence into "excluded".
7	5. One row per real person per document. Relatives described in the document are their own rows with is_proband = false unless the document calls them probands. Do not merge people, and do not create a person the document does not describe.
8	6. Cohort tables: when a table lists many patients, extract each patient row separately with the table's own patient identifier as individual_label_in_paper. Keep the row-to-column alignment of the table; when a cell is empty or marked "-", "NA" or "ND", treat it as not reported.
9	7. Re-reports: if the document says that any of its patients were described in an earlier publication, record that statement and the citation in the publications table. Do not drop the patient.
10	8. Do not infer inheritance or zygosity. "de novo" requires that the document states parental testing showed the variant absent in both parents. "heterozygous" requires that the document says so or the gene is described as monoallelic for that person.
11	9. Prefer "not reported" to a plausible guess. Abstention is correct behaviour.

1	PMID: 36064566
2	PMCID: PMC9446712
3	DOI: 10.1186/s12969-022-00735-1
4	Title: TNFAIP3 mutation causing haploinsufficiency of A20 with a hemophagocytic lymphohistiocytosis phenotype: a report of two cases
5	Journal: Pediatric Rheumatology Online Journal (2022)
6	Authors: Aslani Nahid; Asnaashari Kosar; Parvaneh Nima; Shahrooei Mohammad; Sotoudeh-Anvari Maryam; Shahram Farhad; Ziaee Vahid
7	
8	# TNFAIP3 mutation causing haploinsufficiency of A20 with a hemophagocytic lymphohistiocytosis phenotype: a report of two cases
9	
10	## Abstract
11	
12	BackgroundA20 haploinsufficiency (HA20) is a newly introduced autosomal dominant autoinflammatory disorder, also known as Behcet’s-like disease. Some of the most common symptoms of the disease are recurrent oral, genital, and/or gastrointestinal (GI) ulcers, episodic fever, musculoskeletal symptoms, cutaneous lesions, and recurrent infections. Hemophagocytic lymphohistiocytosis (HLH) is a life-threatening condition of multi-organ failure due to excessive immune activation. HLH has been reported in a few HA20 patients. Herein, we report two children with the primary presentation of HLH, with a mutation in TNFAIP3, in favor of HA20.Case presentationsOur first patient was a 4-month-old boy who presented with fever, irritability, pallor, and hepatosplenomegaly. Pancytopenia, elevated ferritin, and decreased fibrinogen levels were found in laboratory evaluation. He was diagnosed with HLH and was treated with methylprednisolone and cyclosporine. Two years later, whole exome sequencing (WES) indicated a mutation in TNFAIP3 at NM_001270507: exon3: c.C386T, p.T129M, consistent with A20 haploinsufficiency. Etanercept, a TNF inhibitor, was prescribed, but the parents were reluctant to initiate the therapy. The patient passed away with the clinical picture of cerebral hemorrhage.The second patient was a 3-month-old boy who presented with a fever and hepatosplenomegaly. Laboratory evaluation found pancytopenia, hyperferritinemia, hypoalbuminemia, hypertriglyceridemia, and hypofibrinogenemia. With the establishment of the HLH diagnosis, he was treated with etoposide, dexamethasone, and cyclosporine, and recovered. WES results revealed a heterozygous de novo variant of TNFAIP3 (c. T824C in exon 6, 6q23.3) that leads to a proline to leucine amino acid change (p. L275P). He was treated with etanercept and has been symptom-free afterward.ConclusionsThis report is a hypothesis for developing of the HLH phenotype in the presence of TNFAIP3 mutation. Our results provide a new perspective on the role of TNFAIP3 mutation in HLH phenotypes, but more extensive studies are required to confirm these preliminary results.
13	
14	## Background
15	
16	Hemophagocytic lymphohistiocytosis (HLH) is a life-threatening condition of multi-organ failure due to excessive immune activation. It can be presented at all ages but is most frequently reported in infants, occurring as a single or multiple recurring episodes. Fever, splenomegaly, cytopenia, hypertriglyceridemia, hypofibrinogenemia, and hemophagocytosis constitute the criteria for diagnosis of HLH [1]. HLH can be sporadic or happen in the context of a genetic disorder. In both circumstances, infection is the most common trigger [2]. Some genes are found to be associated with familial HLH [3]. Moreover, diseases that alter the immunologic function, such as immunodeficiencies and autoinflammatory syndromes, can be potential causes of HLH [4].
17	
18	A20 haploinsufficiency (HA20) is a newly introduced autosomal dominant autoinflammatory disorder [5]. TNF alpha-induced protein 3 (TNFAIP3) encodes protein A20, an essential negative regulator of nuclear factor–κB (NF-κB)-mediated inflammation. A20 is an E3-ligase that also possesses deubiquitinase activity [6]. HA20, due to reduced protein levels, leads to increased activation in response to tumor necrosis factor α (TNF-α) and toll-like receptor (TLR) stimulation. Heterozygous loss-of-function mutations in A20 cause HA20 and Behcet’s-like disease in children [7].
19	
20	HA20 resembles Behcet’s disease in some symptoms; however, some features in specific individuals lead to an initial diagnosis of atypical systemic lupus erythematosus with central nervous system vasculitis, anterior uveitis, colon ulcers, and autoimmune lymphoproliferative syndrome (ALPS) phenotype [8, 9]. Features of the disease include recurrent oral, genital, and/or gastrointestinal (GI) ulcers, episodic fever, musculoskeletal symptoms, cutaneous lesions, and recurrent infections. Patients with TNFAIP3 mutation can develop autoantibodies. Fluctuating levels of low-titer autoantibodies, including antinuclear antibodies, anti-double-stranded DNA (dsDNA), anti-Sm/ribonucleoprotein (RNP), anticardiolipin, and lupus anticoagulant, were found in the largest reported cohort [10–12]. Acute phase reactants tend to elevate with disease flares, but their levels are normal between flares, which is a characteristic of autoinflammatory syndromes [10].
21	
22	The diagnosis of HA20 based on clinical symptoms is challenging due to various clinical manifestations in different patients. Therefore, the final diagnosis should be confirmed by genetic study and finding of TNFAIP3 mutation [10, 13, 14].
23	
24	The scarcity of reported and published cases of HA20 and unknown presentations of the disease necessitate reporting the diagnosed cases of HA20 and sharing knowledge and experience in this area. Herein, we present a case of genetically confirmed HA20 with the primary presentation of HLH.
25	
26	## Case presentations
27	
28	### Patient one
29	
30	Our patient was referred for the first time at the age of 4 months with the complaint of irritability, pallor, and intermittent fever. He had been admitted to another center for 3 weeks with lethargy, where packed cells and platelets were transfused due to the patient’s pancytopenia. Upon physical examination, the patient was conscious but irritable and appeared pale. The vital signs yielded normal results. His weight and height were appropriate for his age. Hepatosplenomegaly was found when palpating the abdomen. No other abnormality was found.
31	
32	The patient was the son of two cousins, born by a normal vaginal delivery (NVD) after a normal pregnancy. He had reached developmental milestones. He had an older sister who was healthy. There was no family history of serious illnesses or early deaths.
33	
34	Laboratory exams showed that the patient had pancytopenia. Hypochromia and target cells were found on the peripheral blood smear (PBS). He had normal ESR, CRP, and procalcitonin levels. Urine analysis and stool exam were normal, as well as urine, stool, and blood cultures. Rubella, cytomegalovirus (CMV), Toxoplasma, and Epstein-Barr virus (EBV) Immunoglobulin M (IgM) were negative. Considering the laboratory findings, sepsis could be ruled out. We also found a negative fluorescent antinuclear antibody (FANA) value.
35	
36	Due to the findings of fever, splenomegaly, and cytopenia, HLH was a probable diagnosis. Cholesterol and triglyceride levels were checked, with results of 204 mg/dl and 687 mg/dl, respectively. AST, ALT, and ALP levels were mildly elevated. PT was normal, but PTT was elevated. Ferritin level was highly elevated, and fibrinogen level was decreased. Normal numbers of CD3+ T cell, CD4+ T cell, CD8+ T cell, CD16/56+ NK cell, and CD19+ B cell were found by flow cytometry. Nitroblue tetrazolium (NBT) test was also normal. The laboratory data are summarized in Table 1.
37	
38	### Table 1: Laboratory findings of the patient at presentation
39	
40	| Laboratory parameter | Result | Normal Range | Laboratory parameter | Result | Normal Range |
41	|---|---|---|---|---|---|
42	| White Blood Cells | 3.4* | 4-10 (*10^9/L) | Triglyceride | 687* | <150(mg/dL) |
43	| Neutrophil | 2.6 | 2-7(*10^9/L) | Cholesterol | 204 | <200(mg/dL) |
44	| Lymphocyte | 0.6* | 0.8-4(*10^9/L) | PT | 13 | 9.5-13.5(s) |
45	| Hemoglobin | 9.2* | 11-13.5(g/dL) | PTT | 50 | 30-45(s) |
46	| Platelets | 83000* | 150-450(*10^9/L) | INR | 1 | <1.2 |
47	| Ferritin | 3740* | 30-220(ug/L) | Procalcitonin | 0.2 | <0.1 (ng/ml) |
48	| Fibrinogen | 67* | 150-350(mg/dL) | AST | 62* | 10-31(IU/L) |
49	| ESR | 11 | 0-10(mm/hr) | ALT | 43* | 10-31(IU/L) |
50	| CRP | 6 | <6(mg/dL) | ALP | 1328 | 180-1200(IU/L) |
51	
52	Table notes: Asterisk point to the laboratory changes in favor of HLH ESR Erythrocyte sedimentation rate test, CRP C-reactive protein, PT prothrombin time, PTT Partial thromboplastin time, INR International normalized ratio, AST Aspartate aminotransferase, ALT Alanine aminotransferase, ALP Alkaline phosphatase
53	
54	The parents showed us a report of previous bone marrow aspiration, which was interpreted as probable HLH. We repeated the bone marrow aspiration, but the result was inconclusive. Hepatomegaly and splenomegaly were confirmed by sonography. Echocardiography interpretation was normal.
55	
56	Since the HLH criteria were met according to HLH protocol 2004 [15] (fever, splenomegaly, cytopenia, hypertriglyceridemia, hyperferritinemia), methylprednisolone pulse therapy (30 mg/kg) was ordered for three doses in 3 days. Intravenous etoposide (5 mg/kg/dose for three doses) and oral cyclosporine (5 mg/kg/day divided into two doses) were also prescribed. After a week, the patient’s condition improved and the ferritin level decreased. The patient was discharged with a prescription of oral dexamethasone (1 mg three times a day) and cyclosporine (5 mg/kg/day divided into two doses).
57	
58	When the patient was 2 years and 4 months old, the whole exome sequencing (WES) result was delivered to the parents. It indicated a mutation in TNFAIP3 at NM_001270507: exon3: c.C386T, which leads to amino acid change p.T129M, consistent with A20 haploinsufficiency. By that time, the patient was receiving etoposide every 2 weeks, oral dexamethasone (0.5 mg three times a day), and cotrimoxazole syrup (150 mg/m^2/day three times a week), and the treatment had never been stopped since the first presentation of HLH at 4 months up to this point. Etanercept, as a TNF inhibitor, was prescribed. The family went back to their home city and did not initiate the treatment, apparently due to the high cost of the drug. We were later informed that before taking the new therapy, the patient became feverish and thrombocytopenic. He was admitted to a hospital in his home city. His condition rapidly deteriorated, and he had cerebral hemorrhage, which led to a loss of consciousness. He was comatose for 25 days and unfortunately passed away.
59	
60	### Patient two
61	
62	The patient was a 3-month-old boy admitted for a prolonged fever that had lasted for 2 weeks. The pregnancy was uncomplicated, and the infant was the first child of parents who were not related. On examination, the vital signs were stable. He had no syndromic features. The skin appeared normal. BCG vaccination scar and tonsils appeared normal. Hepatosplenomegaly was found. Laboratory findings before treatment are shown in Table 2. The peripheral blood smear showed a macrocytic picture, and the coagulation profile was normal, except for thrombocytopenia. Cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) analysis was normal (WBC = 0, RBC = 0, protein:20 mg/dl, glucose:60 mg/dl) and blood and CSF cultures were negative. In bone marrow aspiration, the hemophagocytosis picture was not detected. By considering the constellation of findings (i.e., fever, hepatomegaly, splenomegaly, pancytopenia, hyperferritinemia, hypoalbuminemia, hypertriglyceridemia, and hypofibrinogenemia, a provisional diagnosis of HLH was made.
63	
64	### Table 2: Laboratory findings of the second patient before treatment and four weeks after treatment
65	
66	| Laboratory Parameter | Before treatment | After treatment | Normal Range |
67	|---|---|---|---|
68	| White Blood Cells | 960* | 6510 | 4-10 (*10^9/L) |
69	| Neutrophil count | 240* (25.1%) | 2930 (42%) | 2-7(*10^9/L) |
70	| Lymphocyte count | 510* (53.1%) | 2620 (40.2%) | 0.8-4(*10^9/L) |
71	| Monocyte count | 140 (20.8%) | 920 (14%) | 120-800(*10^9/L) |
72	| Hemoglobin | 7.8* | 9.7 | 11-13.5(g/dL) |
73	| Platelets | 13,000* | 240,000 | 150-450(*10^9/L) |
74	| ESR | 40 | 24 | 0-10(mm/hr) |
75	| CRP | 101 | 45 | <6(mg/dL) |
76	| AST | 89* | 51 | 10-31(IU/L) |
77	| ALT | 52* | 42 | 10-31(IU/L) |
78	| Triglyceride | 508* | 110 | <150(mg/dL) |
79	| LDH | 1200* | 270 | 105-333(IU/l) |
80	| Ferritin | 8490* | 182 | 30-220(ug/L) |
81	| Fibrinogen | 93* | 453 | 150-350(mg/dL) |
82	
83	Table notes: Asterisk points to the laboratory changes in favor of HLH ESR Erythrocyte sedimentation rate test, CRP C-reactive protein, AST Aspartate aminotransferase, ALT Alanine aminotransferase, LDH Lactate dehydrogenase
84	
85	Additional evaluations were performed to find the etiology of HLH in the patient. Serologic results (IgM and IgG) of CMV, toxoplasmosis, rubella, and human immunodeficiency virus (HIV) were within normal limits. Blood viral loads of EBV and CMV were undetectable, and the urine CMV load was 1975 copies/mL. Evaluation for leishmaniosis, brucellosis, tuberculosis, and mycoplasma yielded negative results.
86	
87	Regarding the immunological evaluation, NBT was 100%. Normal numbers of CD3+ T cell, CD4+ T cell, CD8+ T cell, CD16/56+ NK cell, and CD19+ B cell were found by flow cytometry. The immunoglobulin levels were within normal limits. The metabolic evaluation was normal. FANA was normal. Since no underlying condition could be found for HLH, familial HLH (FHL) was confirmed, and molecular diagnosis (WES test) was indicated. It was performed on the NovaSeq 6000 platform with a reading length of 150 base pairs (bp), library type: SureSelect V6-Post, coverage of 100X, and paired-end sequencing on the extracted DNA from the peripheral blood of the patient and his parents.
88	
89	The treatment with etoposide, dexamethasone, and cyclosporine A was started based on the HLH Guideline (2004), and a course of treatment with ganciclovir was also administered. About 4 weeks after the treatment, the spleen and liver returned to normal size, and laboratory findings showed nearly normal levels (Table 2).
90	
91	WES results were prepared at this time. It identified a heterozygous de novo variant of TNFAIP3 (c. T824C in exon 6, 6q23.3) that leads to a proline to leucine amino acid change (p. L275P), and the CADD score was 29.1. This missense mutation has not been reported in the Human Gene Mutation Database (http://www.hgmd.cf.ac.uk/ac/all.php) and ClinVar Miner (https://clinvarminer.genetics.utah.edu). Sorting Intolerant from Tolerant (https://sift.bii.a-star.edu.sg) and PolyPhen-2 (http://genetics.bwh. harvard.edu/pph2/index.shtml) tools predicted this variant as probably deleterious. Sanger sequencing confirmed that the patient is heterozygous for this de novo mutation, while his parents are homozygous wild type.
92	
93	Based on the genetic study, treatment changed to TNF-α inhibitor (etanercept) with a dose of 0.8 mg/kg per week subcutaneously, and cyclosporine A and corticosteroid were gradually discontinued. After 2 months of treatment with etanercept, leukocytosis and thrombocytosis were resolved, and erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR), C-reactive protein (CRP), serum ferritin, and liver enzymes gradually returned to normal values. After 6 months, he had normal growth and controlled systemic symptoms of inflammation with normal laboratory findings. At the time of writing this report, 4 years have passed since the first presentation of the disease. The patient has been completely symptom-free and is receiving etanercept every 2 weeks.
94	
95	## Discussion
96	
97	In this article, we have reported two cases of HA20 due to TNFAIP3 mutation that primarily manifested in early infancy with HLH. We explained the symptoms, laboratory evaluations, and treatments of these patients.
98	
99	HLH is classified into familial (primary) and acquired (secondary) types [16]. Familial erythrophagocytic lymphohistiocytosis (FEL or FHL) is an autosomal recessive disease that in some patients is associated with decreased apoptosis triggering [17]. There are five subtypes of FHL: FHL type 1 is unknown in gene and its chromosomal location; FHL type 2 includes perforin gene (perforin 1 [PRF1], located at 10q21-22) mutation; FHL type 3 has the Munc 13-4 gene (unc-13 homolog D (UNC13D), located at 17q25) mutation; FHL type 4 includes mutations in STX11 (located at 6q24); and FHL type 5 has Munc 18-2 gene (syntaxin binding protein 2 [STXBP2], located at 19p13) mutation. Despite the name of FHL, the family history is often negative since the disease has recessive inheritance [18].
100	
101	Many conditions can lead to the clinical manifestation of acquired HLH, including malignancies (leukemia, lymphoma, and other solid tumors), infections (viral, bacterial, or parasitic), and rheumatoid disorders [1]. Viral infections, especially Epstein-Barr virus (EBV), may trigger primary as well as secondary HLH [19]. Macrophage activation syndrome (MAS), which is defined as HLH associated with rheumatologic diseases, can be categorized as secondary HLH. Both of our patients met the European League Against Rheumatism (EULAR) Executive Committee and the American College of Rheumatology (ACR) criteria of MAS [20]. It should be noted that our first patient had anemia, yet the level of hemoglobin was 9.2 g/dl. The threshold for anemia in HLH criteria 2004 is 9 g/dl and it might be suggested that all five HLH criteria were not met in the first patient. Therefore, we suggest that the condition here be named as HLH/MAS.
102	
103	High levels of IFN-γ are sufficient to induce many of the disease-associated hallmarks associated with autoinflammatory syndromes, including some of those associated with HLH. Some cytokines contribute to the pathogenesis of MAS, such as IFN-γ-producing CD8+ lymphocytes and TNF-α- and IL-6-producing macrophages [18, 21].
104	
105	TNFAIP3 (OMIMI: 191163) on chromosome 6q23 encodes the A20 protein, which is a negative regulator of the TNF-nuclear factor-kB signaling pathway. Heterozygous mutation in TNFAIP3 leads to the autoinflammatory syndrome: familial Behcet’s-like disease [22]. This mutation has a vertical pattern in some families, consistent with autosomal dominant inheritance with a 50% probability of transfer from parents to their children.
106	
107	In vitro experiments, in which mutant forms of the protein were overexpressed, did not lead to suppression of NF-κB activation. Cell types, which are affected by A20 deficiency in humans, include non-immune cells, such as skin fibroblasts and PBMC, monocyte-derived macrophages, and T cells, the latter of which can be induced to express excess pro-inflammatory cytokines, such as interleukin 9 (IL-9) and IL-17. Additionally, spontaneous NLR family pyrin domain containing 3 (NLRP3) inflammasome activity has been observed in cells from HA20 patients, expressing increased pro-IL-1β. As demonstrated by tumor necrosis factor receptor (TNFR) and IL-1R signaling blockade, the activity of these pathways is essential to maintain active disease [5].
108	
109	Recurrent oral and genital aphthosis, GI ulcers, skin lesions, intermittent fever, ocular lesions, musculoskeletal involvement, vasculitis, neurologic symptoms, and recurrent infections are described in HA20 patients [23]. Although HA20 was first described by Zhou et al. as an autoinflammatory disorder, studies have found autoimmune-like features for the disease [22, 24]. Moreover, each patient seems to have a unique scenario. The three patients that Zhang et al. described in 2021, for instance, have their spectacular stories [25]. One patient presented with intermittent fever, diarrhea which was at times bloody, and monoarthritis which progressed into polyarthritis. The second patient manifested thoracic kyphosis, recurrent oral ulcers, and autoimmune hemolytic anemia. The third patient was referred for intermittent fever and perianal abscesses. The key to the diagnosis of many of the diagnosed cases of HA20 has been a genetic analysis in cases with obscure diagnoses. That is why reporting the cases of HA20 is mandatory for providing insights into diagnosis by summing up the presentations and laboratory evaluations.
110	
111	It has been reported that several autoimmune and inflammatory disorders, including rheumatoid arthritis, systemic lupus erythematosus, psoriasis, inflammatory bowel disease, Crohn’s disease, Behcet’s disease, and type 1 diabetes, are associated with TNFAIP3 polymorphisms [5, 16, 26–28]. Our patients did not have any symptoms of Behcet’s-like or other autoimmune disorders in the first presentation and subsequent follow-ups, but their primary presentation was systemic inflammation. In addition, we did not find any positive autoantibodies, such as antinuclear antibodies, anti-dsDNA, anti-Sm/RNP, anticardiolipin, and lupus anticoagulant in our patients.
112	
113	One of the unexpected presentations of HA20 is HLH. In case series of Li et al. [29], where four HA20 patients with various phenotypes are introduced, one patient is presented with macrophage activation syndrome (MAS), which is a subset of HLH. The patient had a fever, hyperferritinemia, hypertriglyceridemia, and hypofibrinogenemia. She had the c.259C > T (p.R87X) mutation in the TNFAIP3 gene (RS: NM_006290). This was the first report of HA20 patients presenting with MAS. Our patients also fulfilled the criteria for HLH. Since there are many etiologies for this catastrophic phenomenon, establishing the diagnosis at the time of presentation was impossible without genetic analysis.
114	
115	Takagi et al. reported a case of a 7-month-old Japanese boy who developed a fever, skin rash, and hepatosplenomegaly with pancytopenia. The patient’s double negative T (DNT) cells were 5.1% of TCRαβ-positive cells. Immunological data and the patient’s phenotype supported the diagnosis of ALPS. In WES analysis, mutations associated with ALPS-1-like phenotypes were not identified, and de novo mutation of TNFAIP3 was detected [9]. Likewise this case, hepatosplenomegaly and pancytopenia in our patients were the primary presentations. Schulert et al. have also found a possible role for TNFAIP3 in immune dysregulation associated with HLH/MAS [30]. The patients introduced in literature with TNFAIP3 mutation and presentation of HLH/MAS are presented in Table 3.

127	
128	A20 has a crucial role in downregulating NF-κB activity. Inflammatory cytokines such as tumor necrosis factor-α (TNF-α) and interleukin-1β1 (IL-1β1) impose their effects through the activity of NF-κB transcription factors. Failure to suppress NF-κB transcriptional activity results in chronic inflammation and cell death [6, 31]. Moreover, A20 is a negative regulator of NLRP3 inflammasome; deficiency of A20 triggers caspase-8-dependent enhancement of NLRP3 inflammasome activation [32–34]. Therefore, haploinsufficiency of A20, through the mechanisms of NF-κB overactivation and NLRP3 inflammasome, results in the overproduction of proinflammatory cytokines such as IL-1β, IL-6, IL-18, and TNF-α [14]. This state of cytokine storm is what we observe in the setting of HLH [35].
129	
130	There is currently no standard treatment protocol for HA20. Nearly half of the patients were reported to respond well to colchicine, especially when used in combination with immunosuppressive or biological agents. Earlier initiation of biologic agents can possibly reduce the need for long-term glucocorticoid treatments [11, 14]. Therefore, the subsequent treatment plan for patients with such a specific mutation, after the initial control of inflammation, will be biological drugs, primarily anti-TNF and especially etanercept. Hematopoietic stem cell transplantation has been reported effective in patients with severe disease and cerebral vasculitis [10, 11]. Our first patient was receiving etoposide and oral corticosteroid before we got access to his genetic test, and then we prescribed etanercept as an anti-TNF drug. Unfortunately, his condition deteriorated before he had the time to begin the new therapy, and he passed away. In the case of our second patient, however, the genetic results were fortunately available just in time, and he received etanercept, which seems to have ceased the progression of the disease. We chose etanercept because it was more accessible in comparison with other biologics and since it was recommended in the literature, and continued it due to the favorable response in the patient.
131	
132	The primary goal of treating secondary HLH is triggering the cause such as infection, malignancy, autoimmune disease, or autoinflammatory disorder. Moreover, it might be necessary to treat hyperinflammation apart from the etiology. Dexamethasone, etoposide, and cytokine inhibitors have been frequently used for that matter [15, 36]. The recombinant IL-1 receptor antagonist, anakinra [37], the anti-IL-6R antibody, tocilizumab [38], and the JAK inhibitor, ruxolitinib [36], are some of the biologic drugs that have been efficient in treating HLH/MAS. Considering the fact that TNFAIP3 mutation can be associated with HLH, and that HA20 can be presented with the symptoms of HLH/MAS, the biologic drugs seem to be the most reasonable choice for treatment of HA20 when HA20 is a possible trigger of HLH or is in differential diagnosis.
133	
134	## Conclusions
135	
136	This report is a hypothesis for developing of the HLH phenotype in the presence of TNFAIP3 mutation. Our results provide a new perspective on the role of TNFAIP3 mutation in HLH phenotypes, but more extensive studies are required to confirm these preliminary results.

messages.content: 111	It has been reported that several autoimmune and inflammatory disorders, including rheumatoid arthritis, systemic lupus erythematosus, psoriasis, inflammatory bowel disease, Crohn’s disease, Behcet’s disease, and type 1 diabetes, are associated with TNFAIP3 polymorphisms [5, 16, 26–28]. Our patients did not have any symptoms of Behcet’s-like or other autoimmune disorders in the first presentation and subsequent follow-ups, but their primary presentation was systemic inflammation. In addition, we did not find any positive autoantibodies, such as antinuclear antibodies, anti-dsDNA, anti-Sm/RNP, anticardiolipin, and lupus anticoagulant in our patients.

115	Takagi et al. reported a case of a 7-month-old Japanese boy who developed a fever, skin rash, and hepatosplenomegaly with pancytopenia. The patient’s double negative T (DNT) cells were 5.1% of TCRαβ-positive cells. Immunological data and the patient’s phenotype supported the diagnosis of ALPS. In WES analysis, mutations associated with ALPS-1-like phenotypes were not identified, and de novo mutation of TNFAIP3 was detected [9]. Likewise this case, hepatosplenomegaly and pancytopenia in our patients were the primary presentations. Schulert et al. have also found a possible role for TNFAIP3 in immune dysregulation associated with HLH/MAS [30]. The patients introduced in literature with TNFAIP3 mutation and presentation of HLH/MAS are presented in Table 3.

12	BackgroundA20 haploinsufficiency (HA20) is a newly introduced autosomal dominant autoinflammatory disorder, also known as Behcet’s-like disease. Some of the most common symptoms of the disease are recurrent oral, genital, and/or gastrointestinal (GI) ulcers, episodic fever, musculoskeletal symptoms, cutaneous lesions, and recurrent infections. Hemophagocytic lymphohistiocytosis (HLH) is a life-threatening condition of multi-organ failure due to excessive immune activation. HLH has been reported in a few HA20 patients. Herein, we report two children with the primary presentation of HLH, with a mutation in TNFAIP3, in favor of HA20.Case presentationsOur first patient was a 4-month-old boy who presented with fever, irritability, pallor, and hepatosplenomegaly. Pancytopenia, elevated ferritin, and decreased fibrinogen levels were found in laboratory evaluation. He was diagnosed with HLH and was treated with methylprednisolone and cyclosporine. Two years later, whole exome sequencing (WES) indicated a mutation in TNFAIP3 at NM_001270507: exon3: c.C386T, p.T129M, consistent with A20 haploinsufficiency. Etanercept, a TNF inhibitor, was prescribed, but the parents were reluctant to initiate the therapy. The patient passed away with the clinical picture of cerebral hemorrhage.The second patient was a 3-month-old boy who presented with a fever and hepatosplenomegaly. Laboratory evaluation found pancytopenia, hyperferritinemia, hypoalbuminemia, hypertriglyceridemia, and hypofibrinogenemia. With the establishment of the HLH diagnosis, he was treated with etoposide, dexamethasone, and cyclosporine, and recovered. WES results revealed a heterozygous de novo variant of TNFAIP3 (c. T824C in exon 6, 6q23.3) that leads to a proline to leucine amino acid change (p. L275P). He was treated with etanercept and has been symptom-free afterward.ConclusionsThis report is a hypothesis for developing of the HLH phenotype in the presence of TNFAIP3 mutation. Our results provide a new perspective on the role of TNFAIP3 mutation in HLH phenotypes, but more extensive studies are required to confirm these preliminary results.
58	When the patient was 2 years and 4 months old, the whole exome sequencing (WES) result was delivered to the parents. It indicated a mutation in TNFAIP3 at NM_001270507: exon3: c.C386T, which leads to amino acid change p.T129M, consistent with A20 haploinsufficiency. By that time, the patient was receiving etoposide every 2 weeks, oral dexamethasone (0.5 mg three times a day), and cotrimoxazole syrup (150 mg/m^2/day three times a week), and the treatment had never been stopped since the first presentation of HLH at 4 months up to this point. Etanercept, as a TNF inhibitor, was prescribed. The family went back to their home city and did not initiate the treatment, apparently due to the high cost of the drug. We were later informed that before taking the new therapy, the patient became feverish and thrombocytopenic. He was admitted to a hospital in his home city. His condition rapidly deteriorated, and he had cerebral hemorrhage, which led to a loss of consciousness. He was comatose for 25 days and unfortunately passed away.

62	The patient was a 3-month-old boy admitted for a prolonged fever that had lasted for 2 weeks. The pregnancy was uncomplicated, and the infant was the first child of parents who were not related. On examination, the vital signs were stable. He had no syndromic features. The skin appeared normal. BCG vaccination scar and tonsils appeared normal. Hepatosplenomegaly was found. Laboratory findings before treatment are shown in Table 2. The peripheral blood smear showed a macrocytic picture, and the coagulation profile was normal, except for thrombocytopenia. Cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) analysis was normal (WBC = 0, RBC = 0, protein:20 mg/dl, glucose:60 mg/dl) and blood and CSF cultures were negative. In bone marrow aspiration, the hemophagocytosis picture was not detected. By considering the constellation of findings (i.e., fever, hepatomegaly, splenomegaly, pancytopenia, hyperferritinemia, hypoalbuminemia, hypertriglyceridemia, and hypofibrinogenemia, a provisional diagnosis of HLH was made.

91	WES results were prepared at this time. It identified a heterozygous de novo variant of TNFAIP3 (c. T824C in exon 6, 6q23.3) that leads to a proline to leucine amino acid change (p. L275P), and the CADD score was 29.1. This missense mutation has not been reported in the Human Gene Mutation Database (http://www.hgmd.cf.ac.uk/ac/all.php) and ClinVar Miner (https://clinvarminer.genetics.utah.edu). Sorting Intolerant from Tolerant (https://sift.bii.a-star.edu.sg) and PolyPhen-2 (http://genetics.bwh. harvard.edu/pph2/index.shtml) tools predicted this variant as probably deleterious. Sanger sequencing confirmed that the patient is heterozygous for this de novo mutation, while his parents are homozygous wild type.

113	One of the unexpected presentations of HA20 is HLH. In case series of Li et al. [29], where four HA20 patients with various phenotypes are introduced, one patient is presented with macrophage activation syndrome (MAS), which is a subset of HLH. The patient had a fever, hyperferritinemia, hypertriglyceridemia, and hypofibrinogenemia. She had the c.259C > T (p.R87X) mutation in the TNFAIP3 gene (RS: NM_006290). This was the first report of HA20 patients presenting with MAS. Our patients also fulfilled the criteria for HLH. Since there are many etiologies for this catastrophic phenomenon, establishing the diagnosis at the time of presentation was impossible without genetic analysis.

messages.content: 12	BackgroundA20 haploinsufficiency (HA20) is a newly introduced autosomal dominant autoinflammatory disorder, also known as Behcet’s-like disease. Some of the most common symptoms of the disease are recurrent oral, genital, and/or gastrointestinal (GI) ulcers, episodic fever, musculoskeletal symptoms, cutaneous lesions, and recurrent infections. Hemophagocytic lymphohistiocytosis (HLH) is a life-threatening condition of multi-organ failure due to excessive immune activation. HLH has been reported in a few HA20 patients. Herein, we report two children with the primary presentation of HLH, with a mutation in TNFAIP3, in favor of HA20.Case presentationsOur first patient was a 4-month-old boy who presented with fever, irritability, pallor, and hepatosplenomegaly. Pancytopenia, elevated ferritin, and decreased fibrinogen levels were found in laboratory evaluation. He was diagnosed with HLH and was treated with methylprednisolone and cyclosporine. Two years later, whole exome sequencing (WES) indicated a mutation in TNFAIP3 at NM_001270507: exon3: c.C386T, p.T129M, consistent with A20 haploinsufficiency. Etanercept, a TNF inhibitor, was prescribed, but the parents were reluctant to initiate the therapy. The patient passed away with the clinical picture of cerebral hemorrhage.The second patient was a 3-month-old boy who presented with a fever and hepatosplenomegaly. Laboratory evaluation found pancytopenia, hyperferritinemia, hypoalbuminemia, hypertriglyceridemia, and hypofibrinogenemia. With the establishment of the HLH diagnosis, he was treated with etoposide, dexamethasone, and cyclosporine, and recovered. WES results revealed a heterozygous de novo variant of TNFAIP3 (c. T824C in exon 6, 6q23.3) that leads to a proline to leucine amino acid change (p. L275P). He was treated with etanercept and has been symptom-free afterward.ConclusionsThis report is a hypothesis for developing of the HLH phenotype in the presence of TNFAIP3 mutation. Our results provide a new perspective on the role of TNFAIP3 mutation in HLH phenotypes, but more extensive studies are required to confirm these preliminary results.

Moreover, each patient seems to have a unique scenario. The three patients that Zhang et al. described in 2021, for instance, have their spectacular stories [25]. 109	Recurrent oral and genital aphthosis, GI ulcers, skin lesions, intermittent fever, ocular lesions, musculoskeletal involvement, vasculitis, neurologic symptoms, and recurrent infections are described in HA20 patients [23]. Although HA20 was first described by Zhou et al. as an autoinflammatory disorder, studies have found autoimmune-like features for the disease [22, 24]. Moreover, each patient seems to have a unique scenario. The three patients that Zhang et al. described in 2021, for instance, have their spectacular stories [25]. One patient presented with intermittent fever, diarrhea which was at times bloody, and monoarthritis which progressed into polyarthritis. The second patient manifested thoracic kyphosis, recurrent oral ulcers, and autoimmune hemolytic anemia. The third patient was referred for intermittent fever and perianal abscesses. The key to the diagnosis of many of the diagnosed cases of HA20 has been a genetic analysis in cases with obscure diagnoses. That is why reporting the cases of HA20 is mandatory for providing insights into diagnosis by summing up the presentations and laboratory evaluations.

12	BackgroundA20 haploinsufficiency (HA20) is a newly introduced autosomal dominant autoinflammatory disorder, also known as Behcet’s-like disease. Some of the most common symptoms of the disease are recurrent oral, genital, and/or gastrointestinal (GI) ulcers, episodic fever, musculoskeletal symptoms, cutaneous lesions, and recurrent infections. Hemophagocytic lymphohistiocytosis (HLH) is a life-threatening condition of multi-organ failure due to excessive immune activation. HLH has been reported in a few HA20 patients. Herein, we report two children with the primary presentation of HLH, with a mutation in TNFAIP3, in favor of HA20.Case presentationsOur first patient was a 4-month-old boy who presented with fever, irritability, pallor, and hepatosplenomegaly. Pancytopenia, elevated ferritin, and decreased fibrinogen levels were found in laboratory evaluation. He was diagnosed with HLH and was treated with methylprednisolone and cyclosporine. Two years later, whole exome sequencing (WES) indicated a mutation in TNFAIP3 at NM_001270507: exon3: c.C386T, p.T129M, consistent with A20 haploinsufficiency. Etanercept, a TNF inhibitor, was prescribed, but the parents were reluctant to initiate the therapy. The patient passed away with the clinical picture of cerebral hemorrhage.The second patient was a 3-month-old boy who presented with a fever and hepatosplenomegaly. Laboratory evaluation found pancytopenia, hyperferritinemia, hypoalbuminemia, hypertriglyceridemia, and hypofibrinogenemia. With the establishment of the HLH diagnosis, he was treated with etoposide, dexamethasone, and cyclosporine, and recovered. WES results revealed a heterozygous de novo variant of TNFAIP3 (c. T824C in exon 6, 6q23.3) that leads to a proline to leucine amino acid change (p. L275P). He was treated with etanercept and has been symptom-free afterward.ConclusionsThis report is a hypothesis for developing of the HLH phenotype in the presence of TNFAIP3 mutation. Our results provide a new perspective on the role of TNFAIP3 mutation in HLH phenotypes, but more extensive studies are required to confirm these preliminary results.

It indicated a mutation in TNFAIP3 at NM_001270507: exon3: c.C386T, which leads to amino acid change p.T129M, consistent with A20 haploinsufficiency. By that time, the patient was receiving etoposide every 2 weeks, oral dexamethasone (0.5 mg three times a day), and cotrimoxazole syrup (150 mg/m^2/day three times a week), and the treatment had never been stopped since the first presentation of HLH at 4 months up to this point. Etanercept, as a TNF inhibitor, was prescribed. The family went back to their home city and did not initiate the treatment, apparently due to the high cost of the drug. We were later informed that before taking the new therapy, the patient became feverish and thrombocytopenic. He was admitted to a hospital in his home city. His condition rapidly deteriorated, and he had cerebral hemorrhage, which led to a loss of consciousness. He was comatose for 25 days and unfortunately passed away.

messages.content: 113	One of the unexpected presentations of HA20 is HLH. In case series of Li et al. [29], where four HA20 patients with various phenotypes are introduced, one patient is presented with macrophage activation syndrome (MAS), which is a subset of HLH. The patient had a fever, hyperferritinemia, hypertriglyceridemia, and hypofibrinogenemia. She had the c.259C > T (p.R87X) mutation in the TNFAIP3 gene (RS: NM_006290). This was the first report of HA20 patients presenting with MAS. Our patients also fulfilled the criteria for HLH. Since there are many etiologies for this catastrophic phenomenon, establishing the diagnosis at the time of presentation was impossible without genetic analysis.

messages.content: 62	The patient was a 3-month-old boy admitted for a prolonged fever that had lasted for 2 weeks. The pregnancy was uncomplicated, and the infant was the first child of parents who were not related. On examination, the vital signs were stable. He had no syndromic features. The skin appeared normal. BCG vaccination scar and tonsils appeared normal. Hepatosplenomegaly was found. Laboratory findings before treatment are shown in Table 2. The peripheral blood smear showed a macrocytic picture, and the coagulation profile was normal, except for thrombocytopenia. Cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) analysis was normal (WBC = 0, RBC = 0, protein:20 mg/dl, glucose:60 mg/dl) and blood and CSF cultures were negative. In bone marrow aspiration, the hemophagocytosis picture was not detected. By considering the constellation of findings (i.e., fever, hepatomegaly, splenomegaly, pancytopenia, hyperferritinemia, hypoalbuminemia, hypertriglyceridemia, and hypofibrinogenemia, a provisional diagnosis of HLH was made.

Upon physical examination, the patient was conscious but irritable and appeared pale. The vital signs yielded normal results. His weight and height were appropriate for his age. 12	BackgroundA20 haploinsufficiency (HA20) is a newly introduced autosomal dominant autoinflammatory disorder, also known as Behcet’s-like disease. Some of the most common symptoms of the disease are recurrent oral, genital, and/or gastrointestinal (GI) ulcers, episodic fever, musculoskeletal symptoms, cutaneous lesions, and recurrent infections. Hemophagocytic lymphohistiocytosis (HLH) is a life-threatening condition of multi-organ failure due to excessive immune activation. HLH has been reported in a few HA20 patients. Herein, we report two children with the primary presentation of HLH, with a mutation in TNFAIP3, in favor of HA20.Case presentationsOur first patient was a 4-month-old boy who presented with fever, irritability, pallor, and hepatosplenomegaly. Pancytopenia, elevated ferritin, and decreased fibrinogen levels were found in laboratory evaluation. He was diagnosed with HLH and was treated with methylprednisolone and cyclosporine. Two years later, whole exome sequencing (WES) indicated a mutation in TNFAIP3 at NM_001270507: exon3: c.C386T, p.T129M, consistent with A20 haploinsufficiency. Etanercept, a TNF inhibitor, was prescribed, but the parents were reluctant to initiate the therapy. The patient passed away with the clinical picture of cerebral hemorrhage.The second patient was a 3-month-old boy who presented with a fever and hepatosplenomegaly. Laboratory evaluation found pancytopenia, hyperferritinemia, hypoalbuminemia, hypertriglyceridemia, and hypofibrinogenemia. With the establishment of the HLH diagnosis, he was treated with etoposide, dexamethasone, and cyclosporine, and recovered. WES results revealed a heterozygous de novo variant of TNFAIP3 (c. T824C in exon 6, 6q23.3) that leads to a proline to leucine amino acid change (p. L275P). He was treated with etanercept and has been symptom-free afterward.ConclusionsThis report is a hypothesis for developing of the HLH phenotype in the presence of TNFAIP3 mutation. Our results provide a new perspective on the role of TNFAIP3 mutation in HLH phenotypes, but more extensive studies are required to confirm these preliminary results.

messages.content: 113	One of the unexpected presentations of HA20 is HLH. In case series of Li et al. [29], where four HA20 patients with various phenotypes are introduced, one patient is presented with macrophage activation syndrome (MAS), which is a subset of HLH. The patient had a fever, hyperferritinemia, hypertriglyceridemia, and hypofibrinogenemia. She had the c.259C > T (p.R87X) mutation in the TNFAIP3 gene (RS: NM_006290). This was the first report of HA20 patients presenting with MAS. Our patients also fulfilled the criteria for HLH. Since there are many etiologies for this catastrophic phenomenon, establishing the diagnosis at the time of presentation was impossible without genetic analysis.

8	# TNFAIP3 mutation causing haploinsufficiency of A20 with a hemophagocytic lymphohistiocytosis phenotype: a report of two cases

58	When the patient was 2 years and 4 months old, the whole exome sequencing (WES) result was delivered to the parents. It indicated a mutation in TNFAIP3 at NM_001270507: exon3: c.C386T, which leads to amino acid change p.T129M, consistent with A20 haploinsufficiency. By that time, the patient was receiving etoposide every 2 weeks, oral dexamethasone (0.5 mg three times a day), and cotrimoxazole syrup (150 mg/m^2/day three times a week), and the treatment had never been stopped since the first presentation of HLH at 4 months up to this point. Etanercept, as a TNF inhibitor, was prescribed. The family went back to their home city and did not initiate the treatment, apparently due to the high cost of the drug. We were later informed that before taking the new therapy, the patient became feverish and thrombocytopenic. He was admitted to a hospital in his home city. His condition rapidly deteriorated, and he had cerebral hemorrhage, which led to a loss of consciousness. He was comatose for 25 days and unfortunately passed away.

30	Our patient was referred for the first time at the age of 4 months with the complaint of irritability, pallor, and intermittent fever. He had been admitted to another center for 3 weeks with lethargy, where packed cells and platelets were transfused due to the patient’s pancytopenia. Upon physical examination, the patient was conscious but irritable and appeared pale. The vital signs yielded normal results. His weight and height were appropriate for his age. Hepatosplenomegaly was found when palpating the abdomen. No other abnormality was found.

messages.content: 62	The patient was a 3-month-old boy admitted for a prolonged fever that had lasted for 2 weeks. The pregnancy was uncomplicated, and the infant was the first child of parents who were not related. On examination, the vital signs were stable. He had no syndromic features. The skin appeared normal. BCG vaccination scar and tonsils appeared normal. Hepatosplenomegaly was found. Laboratory findings before treatment are shown in Table 2. The peripheral blood smear showed a macrocytic picture, and the coagulation profile was normal, except for thrombocytopenia. Cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) analysis was normal (WBC = 0, RBC = 0, protein:20 mg/dl, glucose:60 mg/dl) and blood and CSF cultures were negative. In bone marrow aspiration, the hemophagocytosis picture was not detected. By considering the constellation of findings (i.e., fever, hepatomegaly, splenomegaly, pancytopenia, hyperferritinemia, hypoalbuminemia, hypertriglyceridemia, and hypofibrinogenemia, a provisional diagnosis of HLH was made.

93	Based on the genetic study, treatment changed to TNF-α inhibitor (etanercept) with a dose of 0.8 mg/kg per week subcutaneously, and cyclosporine A and corticosteroid were gradually discontinued. After 2 months of treatment with etanercept, leukocytosis and thrombocytosis were resolved, and erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR), C-reactive protein (CRP), serum ferritin, and liver enzymes gradually returned to normal values. After 6 months, he had normal growth and controlled systemic symptoms of inflammation with normal laboratory findings. At the time of writing this report, 4 years have passed since the first presentation of the disease. The patient has been completely symptom-free and is receiving etanercept every 2 weeks.

109	Recurrent oral and genital aphthosis, GI ulcers, skin lesions, intermittent fever, ocular lesions, musculoskeletal involvement, vasculitis, neurologic symptoms, and recurrent infections are described in HA20 patients [23]. Although HA20 was first described by Zhou et al. as an autoinflammatory disorder, studies have found autoimmune-like features for the disease [22, 24]. Moreover, each patient seems to have a unique scenario. The three patients that Zhang et al. described in 2021, for instance, have their spectacular stories [25]. One patient presented with intermittent fever, diarrhea which was at times bloody, and monoarthritis which progressed into polyarthritis. The second patient manifested thoracic kyphosis, recurrent oral ulcers, and autoimmune hemolytic anemia. The third patient was referred for intermittent fever and perianal abscesses. The key to the diagnosis of many of the diagnosed cases of HA20 has been a genetic analysis in cases with obscure diagnoses. That is why reporting the cases of HA20 is mandatory for providing insights into diagnosis by summing up the presentations and laboratory evaluations.

115	Takagi et al. reported a case of a 7-month-old Japanese boy who developed a fever, skin rash, and hepatosplenomegaly with pancytopenia. The patient’s double negative T (DNT) cells were 5.1% of TCRαβ-positive cells. Immunological data and the patient’s phenotype supported the diagnosis of ALPS. In WES analysis, mutations associated with ALPS-1-like phenotypes were not identified, and de novo mutation of TNFAIP3 was detected [9]. Likewise this case, hepatosplenomegaly and pancytopenia in our patients were the primary presentations. Schulert et al. have also found a possible role for TNFAIP3 in immune dysregulation associated with HLH/MAS [30]. 122	| 2 | Takagi et al | M | 7 M | Fever, hepatosplenomegaly, hyperferritinemia, thrombocytopenia, increased ALT | Skin rash, lymphadenopathy | c.1245_1248del (NM_001270507), p.Gln415fs |

12	BackgroundA20 haploinsufficiency (HA20) is a newly introduced autosomal dominant autoinflammatory disorder, also known as Behcet’s-like disease. Some of the most common symptoms of the disease are recurrent oral, genital, and/or gastrointestinal (GI) ulcers, episodic fever, musculoskeletal symptoms, cutaneous lesions, and recurrent infections. Hemophagocytic lymphohistiocytosis (HLH) is a life-threatening condition of multi-organ failure due to excessive immune activation. HLH has been reported in a few HA20 patients. Herein, we report two children with the primary presentation of HLH, with a mutation in TNFAIP3, in favor of HA20.Case presentationsOur first patient was a 4-month-old boy who presented with fever, irritability, pallor, and hepatosplenomegaly. Pancytopenia, elevated ferritin, and decreased fibrinogen levels were found in laboratory evaluation. He was diagnosed with HLH and was treated with methylprednisolone and cyclosporine. Two years later, whole exome sequencing (WES) indicated a mutation in TNFAIP3 at NM_001270507: exon3: c.C386T, p.T129M, consistent with A20 haploinsufficiency. Etanercept, a TNF inhibitor, was prescribed, but the parents were reluctant to initiate the therapy. The patient passed away with the clinical picture of cerebral hemorrhage.The second patient was a 3-month-old boy who presented with a fever and hepatosplenomegaly. Laboratory evaluation found pancytopenia, hyperferritinemia, hypoalbuminemia, hypertriglyceridemia, and hypofibrinogenemia. With the establishment of the HLH diagnosis, he was treated with etoposide, dexamethasone, and cyclosporine, and recovered. WES results revealed a heterozygous de novo variant of TNFAIP3 (c. T824C in exon 6, 6q23.3) that leads to a proline to leucine amino acid change (p. L275P). He was treated with etanercept and has been symptom-free afterward.ConclusionsThis report is a hypothesis for developing of the HLH phenotype in the presence of TNFAIP3 mutation. Our results provide a new perspective on the role of TNFAIP3 mutation in HLH phenotypes, but more extensive studies are required to confirm these preliminary results.
58	When the patient was 2 years and 4 months old, the whole exome sequencing (WES) result was delivered to the parents. It indicated a mutation in TNFAIP3 at NM_001270507: exon3: c.C386T, which leads to amino acid change p.T129M, consistent with A20 haploinsufficiency.
